newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Western European Union agrees new armaments cooperation.
newsitem.headline: Western European Union agrees new armaments cooperation.

text.p: The European Union's fledgling defence arm agreed on Tuesday to set up a joint arms and development body to help avoid unnecessary duplication in producing weapons systems for NATO's European members.

Defence and foreign ministers from the Western European Union (WEU) approved the plan, mindful of the strain on national defence budgets since the end of the Cold War and wanting to help the EU defence industry match up to U.S. competition.
French Defence Minister Charles Millon, announcing creation of the Western European Armaments Organisation, said it would allow the EU to create a possible future European arms agency.

He said he expected France, Italy, Germany and Britain -- which forged their own more advanced cooperation accord on arms in Strasbourg, France, last week -- would form the "avant garde" group of countries in the WEU accord.
Diplomats said the agreement gave the EU's embryonic defence arm -- which currently opeore substance.
They predicted eventual creation of a joint procurement agency, which could provide economies of scale for the security industry.
"That is a possible outcome, that it would operate through a joint procurement agency," said one diplomat.
"Instead of buying two telephones you buy 20,000 it's cheaper. It's a security issue, but it's also a money issue.".
The WEU said in a statement the body could place contracts with industries and agencies to faciliate the management of research and technology projects.
An underpinning goal of the WEU is to pool arms resources by harmonising requirements and opening up national defence markets to cross-border competition, while strengthening Europe's defence clout.
Millon said further contacts would be held to examine how armaments needs could be harmonised between the 13 participating members and how the agreement would fit into the EU's border free market.
The armaments organisation comprises the 10 members of the WEU -- Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, Italy, Spain, Greece, Portugal and the Netherlands -- plus Norway, Denmark and Turkey.
The body is set to be fully up and running by April 1, 1997.
